en: Sutta Nipāta 3.9 Vāseṭṭha-sutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove.
Now at that time many well-known and highly esteemed brahmin householders were residing at Icchānaṅgala, namely:
the brahmin Caṅkī, the brahmin Tārukkha, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, the brahmin Todeyya, and other well-known and highly esteemed brahmin householders.
Then, as the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were walking and wandering for exercise, this discussion arose between them:
"How, sir, does one become a brahmin?
The young brahmin Bhāradvāja spoke thus:
“Since, sir, he is well-born on both sides, from mother and father, of pure descent back to the seventh generation of ancestors, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth—
to this extent, sir, one is a brahmin.
Thus spoke the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha.
“Since, sir, he is virtuous and endowed with vows,
to that extent, sir, one is a brahmin.
But Bhāradvāja the young brahmin was unable to convince Vāseṭṭha the young brahmin, nor was Vāseṭṭha the young brahmin able to convince Bhāradvāja the young brahmin.
Then the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha addressed the young brahmin Bhāradvāja:
"Sir Bhāradvāja, this ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is staying at Icchānaṅgala in the grove of Icchānaṅgala.
Now, a fine report concerning the venerable Gotama has spread abroad: [that he is a fully enlightened Buddha...]"
‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: awakened, fully enlightened...
Come now, Master Bhāradvāja, let us approach the ascetic Gotama; having approached him, we will ask the ascetic Gotama about this matter.
We shall bear it in mind exactly as the ascetic Gotama explains it to us.”
“Yes, sir,” the young Brahmin Bhāradvāja replied to the young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha.
Then the young Brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha addressed the Blessed One in verses:
“Both of us are recognized and acknowledged as masters of the three Vedas.”
I am Pokkharasāti’s [son],
this young brahmin Tārukkha;
that which has been declared by those possessed of the threefold knowledge—
Therein we are solitary ones,
masters of the analysis of words,
and in recitation we are like teachers.
Regarding this doctrine of birth,
O Gotama, we have a dispute:
"One becomes a brahmin by birth."
"Bhāradvāja," he says;
"And I call [one so] by virtue of his action—
know this, O Seer."
We two were not able to convince one another;
we have come to question you, sir.
Renowned as the "Fully Awakened One," people approach him with palms joined in reverence, just as they do the moon that has passed beyond its waning.
Thus do they praise and revere Gotama in this world—
he who has arisen as the Eye in the world.
We ask Gotama this:
Is one a brahmin by birth,
or does one become so through action?
"Tell us who do not know,
so that we may come to know a brahmin.
"I shall explain this to you," [he said].
"Vāseṭṭha," said the Blessed One,
"the classification of living beings according to their birth, in its successive stages as they truly are."
For births are indeed mutually distinct.
Know even the grasses and trees,
though they do not claim [consciousness] for themselves.
Their gender is determined by birth,
for their births are distinct from one another;
thus it is with insects and moths as well.
Down to the ant and the beetle;
their characteristic is born of birth,
for their births are indeed distinct from one another.
Know also the four-footed creatures,
both small and large;
their gender is born of their species.
For species are indeed mutually distinct;
know them even among those that crawl on their bellies,
the long-backed uragas.
Their gender is determined by birth,
for their births are distinct from one another;
therefore, you should know even the fish.
Or those that range in the water;
their gender is determined by birth,
for their births are indeed distinct from one another.
Therefore, you should also know that among birds that travel by means of wings,
their characteristic marks are innate to their species.
For species are indeed distinct from one another.
Just as among these species,
the characteristic mark is diverse and consists of the nature of each species.
Thus, among humans,
there is no distinct mark based on birth;
it is not by the hair, nor by the head.
Not with the ears, nor with the eyes;
not with the mouth, nor with the nose,
nor with the lips, nor with the eyebrows.
Not with the neck, nor with the shoulders,
not with the belly, nor with the back;
not with the hips, nor with the chest.
Not in a crowded place, nor during sexual intercourse;
not with hands, nor with feet,
nor with fingers, nor with nails.
Neither by the shanks nor by the thighs,
nor by complexion or voice,
is there any mark consisting of birth.
Just as it is in other births,
this [state] is not found among humans, even within their own individual bodies.
And the constituent factors among humans are designated by the term "samaṇa.
For whoever among humans—
He lives off animal husbandry;
know this, Vāseṭṭha:
he is a farmer, not a brahmin.
"Whoever among humans lives by various crafts—
know this, Vāseṭṭha,"
One who lives by a craft is not a brahmin;
for whoever among humans lives by trade is such.
Know this, Vāseṭṭha:
he is a merchant, not a brahmin—
whosoever among men [acts thus].
He lives by means of another's service;
know this, Vāseṭṭha,
he is a servant, not a brahmin.
Whoever among humans lives by what is not given—
know this, Vāseṭṭha, to be so.
This person is no brahmin.
For whoever among men lives by the profession of arms—
Know this, Vāseṭṭha:
one who is merely a warrior among men is not a brahmin. For whoever it may be among humans—
He lives by means of priesthood;
know this, Vāseṭṭha:
he is a sacrificer, not a brahmin.
Whoever among humans enjoys a village or a kingdom—
know this, Vāseṭṭha, to be so.
"This is a king, not a brahmin.
I do not call one a brahmin by birth from a womb or by descent from a mother."
He is called one who merely says "bho" if he possesses anything;
but one who possesses nothing and takes nothing—
Him I call a brahmin: he who,
having severed all fetters,
does not tremble.
One who has transcended attachment and is detached from fetters— him I call a brahmin.
Having cut through the thong and the strap,
Who has cut the tether along with its fastenings,
who has lifted the crossbar— the Buddha—
I call him a brahmin.
He who, without malice, endures abuse, beating, and imprisonment—
his army is the power of patience.
Him I call a brahmin:
one who is free from anger, steadfast in his vows,
virtuous, and free from pride.
One who is self-controlled in his final body—
him I call a brahmin.
Like water on a lotus leaf...
Like a mustard seed on the point of an awl,
he who is not smeared by sensual pleasures—
him I call a brahmin.
He who understands suffering and its destruction right here for himself— him,
the one whose burden is laid down and who is detached, [I call a brahmin].
Him I call a brahmin:
one of profound wisdom, possessed of intelligence,
skilled in discerning the path and the non-path.
One who has attained the supreme goal—
him I call a brahmin. One who does not associate with householders...
With both [robes and alms] provided by those who live as homeless ones,
wandering without a fixed abode and possessing few desires—
him I call a brahmin.
Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
both the timid and the steadfast,
he who neither kills nor causes others to kill—
Him I call a brahmin: one who is unprovoked among those who provoke,
who is extinguished among those who wield the rod of violence.
Among those who grasp, he who is without grasping—
him I call a brahmin.
He from whom lust and hatred have departed...
Pride and hypocrisy have been cast down like mustard seeds from the point of an awl;
him I call a brahmin.
One should utter speech that is gentle, intelligible, and true;
by means of which one does not offend anyone.
Him I call a brahmin:
he who here [in this world], whether long or short, fine or coarse,
pleasant or unpleasant— whatever exists— does not grasp at it.
In this world, he does not take what is not given;
him I call a brahmin.
He for whom no expectations exist—
In this world and in the next,
one who is free from longing and detached— I call him a brahmin.
In whom no attachments exist,
who through higher knowledge is free from doubt,
and who has reached the immersion in the Deathless—
Him I call a brahmin:
he who here has transcended both merit and evil, as well as both attachments.
One who is sorrowless, stainless, and pure—
him I call a brahmin.
Like the moon, stainless and pure.
One whose mind is serene and undisturbed,
in whom delight and becoming are utterly exhausted—
him I call a brahmin.
He has transcended this mire, this difficult path,
this saṃsāra of delusion;
the meditator has crossed over and reached the further shore.
Unshaken, free from doubt,
extinguished through non-clinging—
him I call a brahmin.
The one who, having abandoned sensual desires,
wanders forth as a homeless renunciant—
him whose existence in sense-desire has been utterly exhausted.
Him I call a brahmin: he who,
having abandoned craving here,
wanders as a homeless renunciant.
One whose craving for existence is completely exhausted—
him I call a brahmin.
Having abandoned human bondage,
He has transcended celestial bonds;
one who is detached from all bonds— him I call a brahmin.
Having abandoned both delight and aversion,
become cooled and free from acquisitions—
the Hero who has overcome the entire world.
Him I call a brahmin:
he who fully understands the passing away of beings and their rebirth in every way.
The one who is unattached, the Well-Gone One,
the Awakened One— him I call a brahmin.
Whose destination they do not know,
Gods, gandhabbas, and humans—
him who has destroyed the taints, the Arahant,
him I call a brahmin.
For one who has nothing before, after,
or in between; who possesses nothing and grasps at nothing—
Him I call a brahmin:
a bull, a preeminent hero,
a great seer, a victor.
The one who is unmoving, washed clean, awakened—
him I call a brahmin.
He who knows his former abodes...
He sees both heaven and the states of woe,
and has reached the destruction of birth—
him I call a brahmin.
For this is merely a common designation in the world,
a name and clan fashioned by convention,
arisen from a mere collection.
Established here and there, long nurtured as a latent tendency,
is the resort of views for one who does not know.
Those who do not know speak to us thus:
"One becomes a brahmin by birth.
But one does not become a brahmin by birth.
One does not become a non-Brahmin by birth;
by one’s deeds one becomes a Brahmin,
and by one’s deeds one becomes a non-Brahmin.
By one's work one is a farmer,
by one's work one is a craftsman;
by one's work one is a merchant.
One becomes a merchant through one's actions;
one becomes a thief through one's actions,
and a warrior through one's actions.
One becomes a sacrificer through action;
one also becomes a king through action.
Thus is this, according to reality.
The wise perceive karma;
seeing dependent origination,
they are skilled in the ripening of karma.
By kamma the world revolves,
by kamma beings revolve;
beings are bound by their kamma.
Like the axle of a moving chariot,
[one is worn] by austerity, the holy life,
self-restraint, and self-control.
By this one becomes a brahmin;
this is the supreme brahminhood.
One endowed with the three types of knowledge,
The noble ones have exhausted rebirth;
know this, Vāseṭṭha,
regarding Brahmā and Sakka among those who understand.
When this was said, the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
The Vāseṭṭha Sutta, the ninth.
